questions.q: The primary of a transformer has 400 turns and an induced emf of 120 V. The secondary, on the same core, has 50 turns. What is the emf induced in the secondary?
questions.concept: Equal emf per turn in both windings
questions.why:
One core, one flux, so both windings share the same dΦ/dt and the emf per turn is the same: 120/400 = 0.30 V per turn. Secondary: ε₂ = 50 × 0.30 = 15 V. Equivalently ε₂/ε₁ = N₂/N₁ = 50/400.

960 V inverts the turns ratio, giving the secondary more emf with fewer turns; 120 V assumes the two emfs are equal, which would need equal turns; 0.30 V is the emf per turn, not the emf of the 50-turn winding.

questions.q: An ideal transformer must give 8.0 V from a 240 V supply. Its secondary has 40 turns. How many turns must the primary have?
questions.concept: Turn count from the voltage ratio
questions.why:
V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁, so N₁ = N₂ (V₁/V₂) = 40 × (240/8.0) = 40 × 30 = 1200 turns. Fewer secondary turns than primary: step-down, as an 8.0 V output demands.

30 is the voltage ratio 240/8.0 quoted as a number of turns; 1.3 is 40 × (8.0/240), the ratio inverted; 9600 is 40 × 240 with the division by 8.0 V forgotten.

questions.q: The secondary of an ideal transformer supplies 6.0 V across a 1.5 Ω lamp. The primary is fed from a 120 V supply. What power does the primary draw from the supply?
questions.concept: Power in equals power out
questions.why:
Secondary current I₂ = V₂/R = 6.0/1.5 = 4.0 A, so the secondary power is I₂V₂ = 4.0 × 6.0 = 24 W. Ideal transformer: I₁V₁ = I₂V₂, so the primary draws 24 W (at I₁ = 0.20 A).

480 W multiplies the secondary current by the primary voltage, mixing the two sides; 4.0 W is the secondary current 4.0 A written with the wrong unit; 9.6 × 10³ W is V₁²/R, the power the lamp would take if it were connected straight to 120 V.

questions.q: A real transformer takes 2.0 A at 240 V from the supply and delivers 18 A at 24 V to its load. What is its efficiency?
questions.concept: Efficiency of a real transformer
questions.why:
Power in = I₁V₁ = 2.0 × 240 = 480 W. Power out = I₂V₂ = 18 × 24 = 432 W. Efficiency = 432/480 = 0.90 = 90%; the missing 48 W goes to eddy currents and heating in the windings and core.

100% assumes an ideal transformer, which the numbers contradict; 111% is 480/432, the ratio upside down, and no device delivers more than it takes; 10% is the fraction lost, not the fraction delivered.

questions.q: A load of 8.0 Ω is connected across the secondary of an ideal transformer with N₂/N₁ = 1/5. What resistance does the supply connected to the primary see?
questions.concept: Resistance seen from the primary via the turns ratio
questions.why:
V₁/I₁ = R/(N₂/N₁)² = 8.0/(1/5)² = 8.0/(1/25) = 8.0 × 25 = 200 Ω. A step-down transformer makes a small load look large to the supply.

40 Ω divides by the ratio 1/5 without squaring it; 0.32 Ω multiplies by (1/5)² instead of dividing; 1.6 Ω multiplies by 1/5, the ratio the wrong way and unsquared.

questions.q: A transformer has 100 turns on coil A and 500 turns on coil B. A 250 V a.c. source is connected to coil B and a load to coil A. Treating it as ideal, what voltage appears across the load?
questions.concept: Identifying the primary from the source connection
questions.why:
The primary is whichever coil the source is connected to: coil B, so N₁ = 500 and N₂ = 100. V₂ = V₁ (N₂/N₁) = 250 × (100/500) = 50 V. With N₂ < N₁ this is a step-down connection.

1250 V takes coil A as the primary because it was named first; 250 V ignores the transformer; 10 V divides by the ratio squared, importing the square from the resistance formula into the voltage ratio.

questions.q: At some instant the flux in a transformer core is changing at 0.050 Wb/s. The primary has 200 turns. What is the magnitude of the emf induced in the primary at that instant?
questions.concept: Faraday's law for one winding of a transformer
questions.why:
ε₁ = −N₁ dΦ/dt, so |ε₁| = 200 × 0.050 = 10 V. Wb/s is the same unit as the volt.

0.050 V forgets N and quotes the rate of change of flux itself; 4.0 × 10³ V divides N by the rate instead of multiplying; 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ V divides the rate by N.

questions.q: A 50 Hz supply feeds an ideal step-up transformer with N₂/N₁ = 20. Which quantity is the same on the secondary side as on the primary side?
options: The resistance seen by the source
questions.concept: What a transformer leaves unchanged
questions.why:
All currents and voltages in a transformer have the same frequency as the source: the secondary emf is driven by the same changing flux, cycle for cycle, so the output is still 50 Hz. The voltage is multiplied by 20, the current divided by 20, and a load R looks like R/400 to the source.

Each wrong option names a quantity the turns ratio does change: voltage by N₂/N₁, current by N₁/N₂, resistance by (N₂/N₁)².

questions.q: A generator delivers 20 kW at 500 V. An ideal transformer steps the voltage up to 10 kV for transmission. Calculate the line current before and after, and the factor by which the I²R loss in the line falls.
options: 40 A and 800 A, loss up by 400
40 A and 2.0 A, loss down by 20
40 A and 2.0 A, loss down by 400
questions.concept: Why power is transmitted at high voltage
questions.why:
I = P/V gives 20 000/500 = 40 A before the transformer. An ideal transformer conserves power, I₁V₁ = I₂V₂, so at 10 000 V the current is 20 000/10 000 = 2.0 A. With the same line resistance the loss I²R falls by (2.0/40)² = 1/400.

A factor of 20 forgets the square in I²R; 800 A applies the ratio the wrong way round and would make matters worse; and the loss cannot be unchanged, because it depends on the current, not on the power carried.

questions.q: A real transformer's secondary reads 12.0 V with nothing connected and 11.2 V while supplying 2.0 A. Calculate the resistance of the secondary winding and the percentage of the induced emf lost inside it at this load.
questions.concept: Emf versus terminal voltage in a real secondary
questions.why:
With nothing connected no current flows and nothing is dropped inside, so the open-circuit reading is the induced emf, ε₂ = 12.0 V. Under load V₂ = ε₂ − I₂r, so the internal drop is 12.0 − 11.2 = 0.80 V and r = 0.80/2.0 = 0.40 Ω. The fraction lost is 0.80/12.0 = 6.7%, and an ideal transformer would have r = 0 and no drop at all.

5.6 Ω is 11.2/2.0, the load's resistance rather than the winding's; 0.80 Ω forgets to divide the drop by the current; 7.1% divides the drop by the terminal voltage instead of by the emf.

questions.q: An amplifier delivers maximum power into 1600 Ω, but the loudspeaker is 4.0 Ω. Using V₁/I₁ = R/(N₂/N₁)², find the turns ratio N₂/N₁ of the matching transformer and the power delivered to the speaker when 40 V rms is applied to the primary.
questions.concept: Impedance matching with a transformer
questions.why:
The primary must present 1600 Ω, so (N₂/N₁)² = R/1600 = 4.0/1600 = 1/400 and N₂/N₁ = 1/20, a step-down. Then V₂ = 40 × (1/20) = 2.0 V and P = V₂²/R = 4.0/4.0 = 1.0 W, which the primary side confirms as V₁²/1600 = 1.0 W.

1/400 is the squared ratio left unrooted; 20 inverts the ratio and would put 800 V across the speaker; 400 W applies V₁²/R with the primary voltage across the 4.0 Ω speaker.

questions.q: A transformer core is made of iron rather than air, and that iron is built from thin insulated sheets rather than a solid block. What do these two design choices achieve?
options: The iron stores the magnetic energy; the sheets let heat escape from inside the core
The iron lowers the resistance of the windings; the sheets hold the frequency steady
The iron raises the flux; the sheets increase the effective turns ratio
The iron raises the flux and guides it from one winding to the other; the sheets break up eddy currents
questions.concept: Purpose of the iron core and its lamination
questions.why:
Iron's high permeability greatly increases the flux the primary current produces, and it gives that flux a closed path so almost all of it also threads the secondary, which is what makes the emf per turn equal in both windings. The changing flux also induces emfs in the core metal itself, and in a solid block these drive large circulating eddy currents that heat it and waste power, so cutting the core into insulated sheets breaks those paths while the flux still runs along them.

Lamination has nothing to do with the turns ratio, the frequency or cooling, and the iron does not change the resistance of the windings.

checks.topic:
The Software Testing Life Cycle and Debugging deck.

What software testing is, and why a defined life cycle is needed at all.

The six STLC phases in sequential order, with the specific activities each phase owns, and entry and exit points.

The definition of a test case as inputs, process and expected outputs.

Debugging as the process of identifying and resolving bugs.

Its named methods: code inspection, monitoring, logging, unit, integration and system testing.

And its tool categories: debuggers, trace tools, profilers.

questions.q: Put the STLC phases in order. A: test execution. B: requirement analysis. C: test environment setup. D: test planning. E: test cycle closure. F: test case development.
options: B, D, F, C, A, E
D, B, F, C, A, E
B, D, C, F, A, E
B, F, D, C, A, E
questions.concept: Ordering the STLC phases
questions.why:
The six phases in sequential order are requirement analysis (B), test planning (D), test case development (F), test environment setup (C), test execution (A) and test cycle closure (E). You must know what to test before you can plan, plan before you write cases, write cases before you set up the environment to run them, run them, then close.

D, B, ... plans before deciding what is to be tested; B, D, C, F, ... sets up the environment before the cases that will run in it exist; B, F, D, ... writes test cases before the strategy, cost and duration are defined.

questions.q: Assign each activity to its STLC phase: (i) interviewing stakeholders; (ii) assigning roles to team members; (iii) reviewing the written test cases; (iv) creating the summary report.
options: (i) test planning, (ii) requirement analysis, (iii) test case development, (iv) test execution
(i) requirement analysis, (ii) test planning, (iii) test case development, (iv) test cycle closure
(i) requirement analysis, (ii) test planning, (iii) test execution, (iv) test cycle closure
(i) requirement analysis, (ii) test case development, (iii) test execution, (iv) test cycle closure
questions.concept: Assigning activities to STLC phases
questions.why:
Requirement analysis owns the requirement document review and the stakeholder interview (i). Test planning defines strategy, cost and duration and assigns roles (ii). Test case development is the identification, writing and review of test cases (iii). Test cycle closure creates the summary report and collects feedback (iv).

The first option swaps the first two phases and puts the summary report in execution, whose reporting is of test results, not the closing summary; the third moves case review into execution; the fourth puts role assignment into case development.

questions.q: Test case development has three objectives: identify, write and review the test cases. A team has identified and written all its cases; the review has not been done, and the calendar date planned for the end of the phase has arrived. Which is true?
options: The exit point is reached: the planned time is up
The exit point is reached: test cases exist
The exit point is not reached: an objective is still unmet
The entry point of test execution is reached
questions.concept: Entry and exit points
questions.why:
The exit point of a phase is where the phase ends and all the objectives of the phase have been achieved. Review is one of the three objectives and it is still owed, so the exit point has not been reached, whatever the calendar says.

'Time is up' confuses a date with an objective; 'test cases exist' satisfies two objectives out of three; the next phase cannot be entered while this one has not exited.

questions.q: A test case reads: 'Inputs: 4 and 5. Process: call add(4, 5). Expected output: whatever the function returns.' Which of the three components of a test case is defective?
options: Nothing: it is a complete test case
questions.concept: Components of a test case
questions.why:
A test case specifies the test inputs, the process and the expected outputs. Testing is finding out whether the output the computer gives is the same as the expected output, so the expected output must be fixed before the run: here it should say 9. 'Whatever the function returns' can never fail, so it tests nothing.

The inputs (4 and 5) and the process (call add(4, 5)) are both stated precisely; 'complete' misses that one of the three parts is empty in effect.

questions.q: Name each debugging method: (i) reading the source of a function line by line looking for a fault; (ii) writing every event and message the program produces to a file to be read afterwards; (iii) watching a running system's response times for unusual behaviour.
questions.concept: Naming debugging methods from descriptions
questions.why:
Code inspection is manually reviewing the source code to identify potential bugs (i). Logging is recording events and messages related to the system so they can be used to identify bugs (ii). Monitoring is watching a running system for unusual behaviour or performance issues that indicate bugs (iii).

The second option calls reading source 'monitoring', but monitoring watches a running system; the third swaps logging and monitoring, but recording to a file is logging; the fourth calls reading source 'unit testing', but unit testing runs the unit on test data rather than reading it.

questions.q: A program gives the correct output but takes 40 seconds. The team wants to know which function consumes most of that time. Which debugging tool category is the right one?
questions.concept: Choosing a debugging tool
questions.why:
The three tool categories are debuggers, trace tools and profilers. A profiler measures where a running program spends its time, function by function, which is exactly the question asked.

A debugger stops at a breakpoint and shows variable values, which locates a wrong value rather than a slow function; a trace tool records the sequence of calls, not their cost; code inspection is a method, not a tool, and reading the source will not tell you which function is slow.

questions.q: The specification says the app must email a receipt after payment, and that total_due for a given order is 4500. A test run finds (i) no receipt is ever sent, because no code does it, and (ii) total_due comes back as 4300. Classify each finding by what testing revealed.
options: (i) an error located, (ii) a missing requirement
(i) a missing requirement, (ii) an error located
questions.concept: What testing reveals
questions.why:
Testing lets us locate errors in the program and also confirm whether there are any missing requirements. No code sends the receipt at all: a requirement in the specification is missing from the program (i). The total is computed, but the output differs from the expected output 4500: an error has been located (ii).

The first option swaps them; 'both missing' treats a wrong number as absent functionality; 'both errors' treats absent functionality as a wrong number.

questions.q: A test reports that balance() returned −50 where 0 was expected. A developer then reads the function, finds a < that should be <=, and changes it. Which activity is testing and which is debugging?
options: The report is debugging; the fix is testing
The report is testing; finding and fixing the < is debugging
questions.concept: Testing versus debugging
questions.why:
Software testing is the process of finding out whether the output the computer gives is the same as the expected output: the report of −50 against 0 is testing, and it hands over a symptom. Debugging is the process of identifying and resolving errors: finding the < and changing it supplies the cause and the fix.

The other options either merge the two processes or reverse them; the test finds that something is wrong, the debugging finds what and repairs it.

questions.q: pct(score, total) must return score/total × 100 rounded to the nearest whole number, and must return 0 when total is 0. What are the expected outputs of test cases for pct(45, 60) and for pct(3, 0)?
questions.concept: Writing a test case
questions.why:
The expected output of a test case is fixed from the specification before anything is run. 45 / 60 = 0.75, and × 100 gives 75. For a zero total the specification gives the answer outright: 0, with no division attempted.

0.75 forgets the × 100; expecting an error for pct(3, 0) predicts what the code will probably do instead of what the specification requires, which is the one thing a test case must not do.

questions.q: A team finishes test case development and goes straight to test execution, skipping test environment setup. Which problem does that skip cause?
options: A case needing a customer with an overdue loan cannot run, because no such test data exists.
There are no test cases to run, because none have been written.
Nobody knows who runs which test, because roles were never assigned.
There is no summary report at the end, because nothing was recorded.
questions.concept: Consequences of skipping an STLC phase
questions.why:
Test environment setup is where the software and hardware requirements are specified and the test data and the environment are prepared. Skipping it leaves the cases with nothing to run against: the accounts, loans and records they assume do not exist, and any failure cannot be told apart from a version mismatch in the environment.

Writing the cases belongs to test case development, assigning roles to test planning and the summary report to test cycle closure, so none of those three follows from this skip.

questions.q: A program crashes about once a day at an unpredictable moment and nobody has ever seen it happen. Which two debugging methods should be applied first?
questions.concept: Choosing debugging methods for a fault
questions.why:
Nobody is watching when it happens, so the first job is to record what the program was doing. Logging writes the events and messages to a file that can be read after the crash, and monitoring watches the running system for unusual behaviour, such as memory climbing towards the moment of failure.

Unit testing needs a known function and fixed inputs, which a once-a-day condition is unlikely to reproduce; code inspection needs a place in the source to start reading, which only the log can point to; and the integration and system levels test a build, not a rare run-time event.

questions.q: A team tests with no defined life cycle: each tester runs whatever checks seem useful and everyone stops on the release date. What does a defined testing life cycle give them that this does not?
options: A guarantee that the software contains no defects at all.
A way of testing without writing test cases in advance.
Fewer testers, because the phases all run at the same time.
Deliverables and objectives for each phase, and an exit point reached only when those objectives are met.
questions.concept: Purpose of a defined testing life cycle
questions.why:
A defined life cycle states the deliverables and objectives of every phase and gives each one an entry point and an exit point, and that exit point is reached when the objectives have been achieved, not when the calendar says so. Stopping on the release date is stopping on time, with no statement of what would have counted as finished.

No process guarantees a defect-free program; the life cycle adds test case development rather than removing it; and its phases run in sequence, so it saves nobody.

checks.topic:
Computation pass on Week 12: evaluating her seven worked examples and close variants of them.

∫₀⁵(2t² + 6t + 1)dt for the car.

x(t) = 2t³ − 3t² − 12t − 4, and the 115 m net displacement.

The dam force 2.94 × 10⁶[x²/2]₀¹⁰⁰. The rope work 0.6468[60x − x²/2]₀⁶⁰.

TR from MR, with TR(2) = 260.

The capital growth 4t^(3/2)|₄⁹ that the slide mis-states.

And the surplus pair CS = 5000 and PS ≈ 5333, for D(Q) = 1000 − 25Q against S(Q) = 100 + Q².

questions.q: A body has velocity v(t) = 3t² − 12 m/s. Find its net displacement over the first 3 seconds.
questions.concept: Net displacement as a signed definite integral
questions.why:
Net displacement = ∫₀³(3t² − 12)dt = [t³ − 12t]₀³ = 27 − 36 = −9 m. The body ends 9 m on the negative side of where it started: v < 0 on (0, 2) (it goes backwards 16 m) and v > 0 on (2, 3) (it comes forward 7 m).

9 m drops the sign, which reverses the direction of the result; 15 m is v(3), the velocity at the end; 23 m is 16 + 7, the total distance travelled, but net displacement is the signed sum, −16 + 7.

questions.q: A rectangular dam is 40 m high and 150 m wide, with its top level with the water surface. Take ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.8 m/s². Find the total fluid force on the dam face.
questions.concept: Fluid force on a rectangular dam
questions.why:
w = ρg = 9800 N/m³, h(x) = x from 0 to 40, L(x) = 150. F = ∫₀⁴⁰9800·x·150 dx = 1 470 000∫₀⁴⁰x dx = 1 470 000[x²/2]₀⁴⁰ = 1 470 000 × 800 = 1.176 × 10⁹ N.

2.352 × 10⁹ N forgets to divide by 2 in [x²/2], equivalent to applying the base pressure to the whole face; 1.2 × 10⁸ N uses ρ = 1000 instead of ρg = 9800; 5.88 × 10⁷ N integrates 1 instead of x, leaving the depth out.

questions.q: A 40 m rope of mass 80 g/m hangs over the edge of a cliff. Take g = 9.8 m/s². Find the work done in pulling the whole rope up to the top.
questions.concept: Work done pulling up a hanging rope
questions.why:
After x m has been pulled up, (40 − x) m still hangs, with mass 0.08(40 − x) kg (80 g/m = 0.08 kg/m), so the force is F(x) = 9.8 × 0.08 × (40 − x) = 0.784(40 − x) N. W = ∫₀⁴⁰0.784(40 − x)dx = 0.784[40x − x²/2]₀⁴⁰ = 0.784(1600 − 800) = 0.784 × 800 = 627.2 J.

1254.4 J is the starting force 31.36 N times 40 m, valid only for a constant force; 627 200 J never converts grams to kilograms; 800 J integrates (40 − x) but drops the coefficient 0.784.

questions.q: A company's marginal revenue is MR(Q) = 200 − 4Q + 3Q², and its total revenue at Q = 1 is 210. Find the total revenue function TR(Q).
questions.concept: Total revenue from marginal revenue with a data point
questions.why:
TR(Q) = ∫(200 − 4Q + 3Q²)dQ = 200Q − 2Q² + Q³ + C. Then TR(1) = 200 − 2 + 1 + C = 199 + C = 210, so C = 11 and TR(Q) = 200Q − 2Q² + Q³ + 11.

+ 210 copies the given revenue straight into C instead of solving 199 + C = 210; 200Q − 4Q² + 3Q³ + 11 fails to divide by the new powers; leaving the constant off gives TR(1) = 199, not 210.

questions.q: The rate of investment is I(t) = 6√t. The capital growth from the 1st year to the Tth year is 104. Find T.
questions.concept: Finding the time from a given capital growth
questions.why:
K = ∫₁ᵀ6t^(1/2)dt = [4t^(3/2)]₁ᵀ = 4T^(3/2) − 4. Set 4T^(3/2) − 4 = 104, so T^(3/2) = 27, and T = 27^(2/3) = (∛27)² = 9. Check: 4(9^(3/2)) − 4 = 4(27) − 4 = 104.

T = 27 stops at T^(3/2) = 27 without undoing the power; T = 3 takes the cube root of 27 but forgets to square it; T = 26 treats t^(3/2) as t and solves 4T − 4 = 100.

questions.q: The demand function is D(Q) = 90 − 3Q and the market equilibrium is Q₀ = 10, P₀ = 60. Find the consumer surplus.
questions.concept: Consumer surplus at a given equilibrium
questions.why:
CS = ∫₀^Q₀[D(Q) − P₀]dQ = ∫₀¹⁰(90 − 3Q − 60)dQ = ∫₀¹⁰(30 − 3Q)dQ = [30Q − 3Q²/2]₀¹⁰ = 300 − 150 = 150.

300 keeps only the 30Q term and drops the −3Q²/2; 750 is ∫₀¹⁰(90 − 3Q)dQ, the total willingness to pay, with the price P₀ never subtracted; 600 is P₀ × Q₀, the amount actually spent.

questions.q: For a product, the demand function is D(Q) = 200 − 12Q and the supply function is S(Q) = 40 + Q². Find the equilibrium quantity Q₀ and price P₀.
questions.concept: Market equilibrium from demand equals supply
questions.why:
Set D(Q) = S(Q): 200 − 12Q = 40 + Q², so Q² + 12Q − 160 = 0, (Q + 20)(Q − 8) = 0, giving Q = 8 or Q = −20. A negative quantity is meaningless, so Q₀ = 8. Then P₀ = D(8) = 200 − 96 = 104, and S(8) = 40 + 64 = 104 confirms it.

Q₀ = −20 takes the negative root; P₀ = 200 is D(0), the price at zero quantity; P₀ = 136 evaluates 200 − 8·8, squaring Q in the demand function.

questions.q: A body has velocity v(t) and ∫₀⁴v(t)dt = 0. Which statement must be true?
options: The body did not move during [0, 4]
The total distance travelled was zero
The body finished where it started
questions.concept: Interpreting a zero net displacement
questions.why:
∫₀⁴v(t)dt = x(4) − x(0) is the net displacement, the change in position. Zero net displacement means x(4) = x(0): the body is back at its starting point. For example, with v(t) = 2t − 4: ∫₀⁴(2t − 4)dt = 16 − 16 = 0, yet the body moves back 4 m and then forward 4 m.

The other three options confuse net displacement with motion: v need not be zero, the body can move, and the distance travelled (8 m in the example) is not zero; only the signed sum of the backward and forward parts is.

questions.q: A resource is consumed at 40e^(0.02t) thousand tonnes per year, t years after 2010, with C(0) = 0. In which year is a reserve of 1000 thousand tonnes exhausted?
questions.concept: Exhaustion time from an exponential consumption model
questions.why:
C(t) = ∫40e^(0.02t)dt = (40/0.02)e^(0.02t) + c = 2000e^(0.02t) + c, and C(0) = 0 gives c = −2000. Set 2000e^(0.02t) − 2000 = 1000, so e^(0.02t) = 1.5 and 0.02t = ln 1.5 = 0.4055, giving t = 20.27 years, that is the year 2030.

2213 divides ln 1.5 by 0.002; 2065 solves e^(0.02t) = 3 by dividing 3000 by 1000 instead of 2000; 2045 solves e^(0.02t) = 2, taking the reserve as the coefficient 2000.

questions.q: The demand function is D(Q) = 250 − 5Q and the supply function is S(Q) = 100 + Q². Find the producer surplus at equilibrium.
questions.concept: Producer surplus after finding equilibrium
questions.why:
Equilibrium: 250 − 5Q = 100 + Q² gives Q² + 5Q − 150 = (Q + 15)(Q − 10) = 0, so Q₀ = 10 after discarding Q = −15, and P₀ = 250 − 50 = 200 (check S(10) = 200). Then PS = ∫₀¹⁰[P₀ − S(Q)]dQ = ∫₀¹⁰(100 − Q²)dQ = [100Q − Q³/3]₀¹⁰ = 1000 − 1000/3 = 2000/3.

250 is the consumer surplus ∫₀¹⁰[D(Q) − P₀]dQ; 1000 drops the −Q³/3 term; 2750/3 integrates D(Q) − S(Q) instead of P₀ − S(Q).

questions.q: A body has velocity v(t) = 3t² − 6t m/s and initial displacement x(0) = 5 m. Find x(t) and the displacement between t = 1 and t = 3.
questions.concept: Position function from velocity and displacement over an interval
questions.why:
x(t) = ∫(3t² − 6t)dt = t³ − 3t² + C, and x(0) = C = 5, so x(t) = t³ − 3t² + 5. The displacement from t = 1 to t = 3 is x(3) − x(1) = 5 − 3 = 2 m, the same as ∫₁³(3t² − 6t)dt = [t³ − 3t²]₁³ = 0 − (−2) = 2 m, since the constant cancels.

The second option never uses x(0) = 5 to fix C; 5 m reports the position x(3) rather than a change; 8 m adds x(3) and x(1) instead of subtracting.

questions.q: In CS = ∫₀^Q₀[D(Q) − P₀]dQ and PS = ∫₀^Q₀[P₀ − S(Q)]dQ, why do both integrals stop at Q₀?
options: Beyond Q₀ the demand and supply curves cross, so the two integrands would cancel
Only Q₀ units are traded: past it no consumer would buy and no producer would sell at P₀
Q₀ is where D(Q) reaches zero, so there is nothing further to add
The integrals converge up to Q₀ and diverge beyond it
questions.concept: Why the surplus integrals stop at the equilibrium quantity
questions.why:
D(Q) is what a consumer would have paid for the Q-th unit and S(Q) is the least a producer would accept for it, while every unit actually changes hands at the single price P₀. So D(Q) − P₀ is the saving on a unit and P₀ − S(Q) is the extra received on it. Only Q₀ units are traded, because beyond Q₀ demand has fallen below P₀ and supply costs more than P₀, so there is no further surplus to add.

The curves cross at Q₀ itself, not beyond it; D(Q₀) = P₀, not 0; and these are ordinary definite integrals, so convergence is not the issue.

checks.topic:
Problems-only session on Week 12 transformers.

Compute with the lecturer's three tools and nothing else. V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁ for turns ratios and voltages. P_av = V₁I₁ together with I₁V₁ = I₂V₂ for currents. And V₁/I₁ = R/(N₂/N₁)² for resistances.

Covers all six part-answers of her two worked examples: 2, 8.0 A, 60 Ω, 1/2, 6.67 A, 36 Ω.

Also the line she leaves out of Example 2(c), fresh numbers on the same three formulas, and one wrong solution to diagnose.

questions.q: A 1200 W appliance designed for a 230 V supply is to be run from a 115 V line through an ideal transformer. What turns ratio N₂/N₁ is needed, and what kind of transformer is it?
questions.concept: Turns ratio from the appliance rating and the line voltage
questions.why:
The line is the primary (V₁ = 115 V) and the appliance is the load on the secondary (V₂ = 230 V). N₂/N₁ = V₂/V₁ = 230/115 = 2. Since N₂ > N₁ it is a step-up transformer.

1/2 puts the appliance's rating on the primary, swapping the two sides; '2, step-down' has the ratio right but the definition wrong, since more secondary turns means step-up; 4 squares the ratio, a square that belongs only in the resistance formula.

questions.q: A 1000 W hair dryer rated for 120 V is run from a 240 V outlet through an ideal transformer. What current does it draw from the outlet?
questions.concept: Line current from the average power
questions.why:
The outlet is the primary, so P_av = V₁I₁ gives I₁ = 1000/240 = 4.17 A, about 4.2 A.

8.3 A is I₂ = 1000/120, the current in the dryer's own element, not what the outlet supplies; 2.1 A halves the line current a second time, applying the 1/2 ratio to a current that was already the primary's; 0.24 A is V/P, the ratio inverted.

questions.q: A 120 V supply connected to the primary of an ideal transformer sees an effective resistance of 12 Ω. The turns ratio is N₂/N₁ = 3. What is the resistance of the load on the secondary?
questions.concept: Load resistance from the resistance seen by the supply
questions.why:
V₁/I₁ = R/(N₂/N₁)², so R = (V₁/I₁)(N₂/N₁)² = 12 × 3² = 12 × 9 = 108 Ω. Check: V₂ = 360 V, I₁ = 10 A so I₂ = 10/3 A, and 360/(10/3) = 108 Ω.

36 Ω multiplies by the ratio 3 instead of by its square; 4.0 Ω divides by the ratio; 1.3 Ω divides by the square, the formula applied backwards.

questions.q: A 1000 W hair dryer rated for 120 V is run from a 240 V outlet through an ideal transformer. What resistance does the dryer appear to have to the 240 V outlet?
questions.concept: Apparent resistance from the supply voltage and current
questions.why:
The apparent resistance is what the supply sees: V₁/I₁ with I₁ = P/V₁ = 1000/240 = 4.17 A, so V₁/I₁ = 240/4.17 = 57.6 Ω, about 58 Ω. Equivalently V₁²/P = 57 600/1000 = 57.6 Ω.

14 Ω is the dryer's own resistance, V₂²/P = 120²/1000 = 14.4 Ω, the answer to a different question; 29 Ω divides 57.6 by the ratio 2 instead of leaving it alone; 115 Ω multiplies it by 2.

questions.q: The secondary of an ideal transformer has 60 turns and gives 9.0 V. The primary has 1600 turns. What voltage is applied to the primary?
questions.concept: Primary voltage from the turns ratio
questions.why:
V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁, so V₁ = V₂ (N₁/N₂) = 9.0 × (1600/60) = 9.0 × 26.7 = 240 V.

9.0 V assumes the voltages are equal; 0.34 V is 9.0 × (60/1600), the ratio inverted, which would make the 1600-turn winding the low-voltage side; 27 V is the turns ratio 1600/60 quoted as a voltage.

questions.q: An ideal transformer has N₂/N₁ = 1/6 and its primary draws 0.50 A. What current flows in the secondary?
questions.concept: Current ratio as the inverse of the turns ratio
questions.why:
I₁V₁ = I₂V₂ and V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁ = 1/6, so I₂ = I₁ (V₁/V₂) = I₁ (N₁/N₂) = 0.50 × 6 = 3.0 A. Stepping the voltage down 6 times steps the current up 6 times.

0.083 A is 0.50/6, applying the turns ratio to the current the same way as to the voltage; 0.50 A assumes the currents are equal, which would lose five sixths of the power; 18 A multiplies by 6², a square that belongs in the resistance formula only.

questions.q: An ideal transformer draws 0.50 A from a 240 V supply. Its secondary feeds a heater of resistance 7.5 Ω. What current flows in the heater?
questions.concept: Secondary current from power and load resistance
questions.why:
Power in = I₁V₁ = 0.50 × 240 = 120 W, and for an ideal transformer this is the power in the heater: I₂²R = 120, so I₂ = √(120/7.5) = √16 = 4.0 A. Check: V₂ = 4.0 × 7.5 = 30 V, and 30 × 4.0 = 120 W.

16 A is P/R without the square root, a current squared; 0.50 A assumes the secondary current equals the primary's; 32 A is V₁/R, connecting the heater straight to 240 V.

questions.q: An ideal step-up transformer doubles the voltage. Compared with the primary, what are the secondary current and the secondary power?
options: Half the current, half the power
questions.concept: Voltage is bought with current
questions.why:
I₁V₁ = I₂V₂ is the whole energy statement: if V₂ = 2V₁ then I₂ = I₁/2, and the power I₂V₂ is unchanged. A transformer redistributes voltage and current; it never adds watts.

'Double the current' would give four times the power out of nothing; 'same current, double the power' likewise creates energy; 'half the power' would mean half the input vanished inside an ideal device, which by definition has no losses.

questions.q: A 720 W appliance rated for 240 V is run from a 120 V line through an ideal transformer. Calculate the current drawn from the line and the appliance's own resistance.
questions.concept: Line current and load resistance in a step-up transformer
questions.why:
The 120 V line feeds the primary, so P = V₁I₁ gives I₁ = 720/120 = 6.0 A. The line sees V₁/I₁ = 20 Ω, and R = (V₁/I₁)(N₂/N₁)² with N₂/N₁ = 240/120 = 2, so R = 20 × 4 = 80 Ω. The secondary side agrees: I₂ = 720/240 = 3.0 A and R = 240/3.0 = 80 Ω.

3.0 A is the current in the appliance, not in the line; 40 Ω leaves the turns ratio unsquared; 20 Ω is the resistance the line sees, not the appliance's own.

questions.q: A 1200 W appliance rated for 110 V is run from a 220 V outlet through an ideal transformer. Calculate the resistance the appliance appears to have to the outlet, and its own resistance.
questions.concept: Apparent versus actual resistance in a step-down
questions.why:
I₁ = P/V₁ = 1200/220 = 5.45 A, so the outlet sees V₁/I₁ = 220/5.45 = 40 Ω. The turns ratio is N₂/N₁ = 110/220 = 1/2, and R = (V₁/I₁)(N₂/N₁)² = 40 × 1/4 = 10 Ω. Check from the other side: I₂ = 1200/110 = 10.9 A and R = 110/10.9 = 10 Ω.

20 Ω uses the ratio without squaring it; 161 Ω divides by (1/2)² instead of multiplying; and swapping the two confuses what the outlet sees with what the appliance is.

questions.q: An ideal transformer has N₂/N₁ = 4, a 30 V rms supply on the primary and a 60 Ω resistor across the secondary. Calculate the primary current and the resistance the supply sees.
questions.concept: Loaded step-up transformer from the supply side
questions.why:
V₂ = V₁(N₂/N₁) = 30 × 4 = 120 V, so I₂ = V₂/R = 120/60 = 2.0 A. Power is conserved, I₁V₁ = I₂V₂, giving I₁ = (2.0)(120)/30 = 8.0 A. The supply therefore sees V₁/I₁ = 30/8.0 = 3.75 Ω, which agrees with R/(N₂/N₁)² = 60/16 = 3.75 Ω.

2.0 A takes the primary current to equal the secondary current; 0.50 A applies the turns ratio to the current the same way as to the voltage; 15 Ω divides R by 4 rather than by 4².

questions.q: A 500 W appliance rated for 250 V runs from a 125 V line through an ideal transformer. A student writes: I₁ = 500/125 = 4.0 A, so V₁/I₁ = 125/4.0 = 31.25 Ω; N₂/N₁ = 2, so the appliance's resistance is 31.25 × 2 = 62.5 Ω. What is the appliance's resistance?
options: 62.5 Ω, and the working is right
31.25 Ω, which is what the line sees
15.6 Ω, the ratio being 1/2 rather than 2
125 Ω, the turns ratio having to be squared
questions.concept: Diagnosing an unsquared turns ratio
questions.why:
The current, the apparent resistance 31.25 Ω and the ratio 2 are all correct; the error is in the last line, because V₁/I₁ = R/(N₂/N₁)² means R = (V₁/I₁)(N₂/N₁)² = 31.25 × 2² = 125 Ω. The secondary side confirms it: I₂ = 500/250 = 2.0 A and R = V₂/I₂ = 250/2.0 = 125 Ω, or V₂²/P = 125 Ω.

62.5 Ω keeps the unsquared ratio; 31.25 Ω is what the line sees, not the appliance; and 1/2 inverts the ratio, since the appliance sits on the higher-voltage side.

checks.topic:
Applying the Software Testing Methods deck to real code.

Classifying a failure as functional or non-functional, then choosing the method: unit, integration, system, acceptance versus usability, performance, security, compatibility.

Choosing the integration direction, top-down or bottom-up.

Deciding between black, white and grey box for a given situation, and knowing which levels each applies to.

Designing test data by equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis.

And reading a debugger's breakpoint and variable watch to name the defect class.

questions.q: Name the functional testing method for each: (i) test data is fed into one function to check each of its execution paths; (ii) after every part is integrated, the whole app is checked against its technical and functional requirements; (iii) the finished app is checked against the expected requirements, including spelling errors and bugs that crash it.
questions.concept: Choosing the functional testing level
questions.why:
Unit testing uses test data to check the execution paths in a function (i). System testing tests the system as a whole after all parts are integrated to confirm it meets the technical and functional requirements (ii). Acceptance testing confirms the software meets the expected requirements and also looks for spelling errors and for bugs that cause major errors and crashes (iii).

The first option calls the whole-app check 'integration', but integration tests how parts work together, not the assembled whole; the second calls a single-function check 'integration'; the fourth swaps system and acceptance.

questions.concept: Choosing inputs to cover execution paths
questions.why:
White box testing chooses inputs to exercise paths through the code. There are three ways out: the first if (x < 0), the second if (even, non-negative), and the final return (odd, non-negative). −1 takes the first, 4 the second, 7 the third: 3 paths, one input each.

2, 4, 6 are all even and non-negative, so they all take the same path and two paths are never run; 2 paths forgets the negative branch; 4 paths counts −2 and −1 as different, but both leave at x < 0 and the parity test is never reached for either.

questions.q: Main calls Report and Pay; Pay calls Tax. The team tests Main first, with placeholders standing in for the modules below it, then Report and Pay, and Tax last. Which integration approach is this?
questions.concept: Integration testing direction
questions.why:
Integration tests check how well different parts work together and can be top-down or bottom-up. With the top-down approach, higher-level modules are tested first before the lower-level modules: Main, then Report and Pay, then Tax.

Bottom-up would start with Tax and finish with Main; system testing tests the whole after everything is integrated, not module by module; unit testing tests one function on its own, not how modules connect.

questions.q: Three testers: (i) never sees the source and works the web pages in a browser, checking outputs against expected outcomes; (ii) reads the implementation and picks inputs to drive each path through the code; (iii) studies the code of two modules to design the cases, then runs them through the exposed interfaces. Classify each.
options: (i) black box, (ii) white box, (iii) grey box
(i) white box, (ii) black box, (iii) grey box
(i) black box, (ii) grey box, (iii) white box
(i) grey box, (ii) white box, (iii) black box
questions.concept: Black, white and grey box
questions.why:
The distinction is what the tester knows of the internal structure. (i) knows nothing of it and tests from outside: black box. (ii) knows the implementation and chooses inputs to exercise paths through the code: white box. (iii) uses internal knowledge to design the cases but tests at the black-box level through the interfaces: grey box, the combination.

The second option swaps the first two; the third calls path-driven testing 'grey', but (ii) tests the code directly, not through interfaces; the fourth calls (iii) black box, but its cases were designed from the source.

questions.q: A field accepts a whole-number score, valid from 0 to 100 inclusive. Which set takes exactly one value from each equivalence class of the input?
questions.concept: Equivalence partitioning
questions.why:
The input splits into three classes the program should treat identically: below the range (score < 0), valid (0 to 100), above the range (score > 100). One representative per class: −5, 50, 120.

{0, 50, 100} takes three values from the valid class and none from the invalid ones; {10, 50, 90} likewise; {−5, −1, 120} takes two from the below-range class and none from the valid class.

questions.q:
fee(days) is specified as: the first day is free, then 50 per extra day, so fee(1) = 0 and fee(3) = 100. Four test cases: A fee(0) expects 0; B fee(1) expects 0; C fee(3) expects 100; D fee(−2) expects 0. Which cases fail against this implementation?

```python
def fee(days):
    if days <= 0:
        return 0
    return 50 * days
```
questions.concept: Running test cases against an implementation
questions.why:
Run each case. fee(0) = 0 and fee(−2) = 0, so A and D pass. fee(1) = 50 × 1 = 50, expected 0: B fails. fee(3) = 50 × 3 = 150, expected 100: C fails. The implementation charges for the free day; the fix is 50 × (days − 1).

'B only' misses that the same defect overcharges every positive input; 'C only' misses the boundary case at 1; 'A and D' are the cases the implementation gets right.

options: Change `for m in marks` to `for m in marks[1:]`
questions.concept: Fixing a wrong relational operator
questions.why:
Step through with the watch: m = 50 fails m > 50, so n stays 0; m = 70 passes, n = 1; m = 30 fails. The mark exactly at the boundary is excluded, so the defect is a wrong relational operator: > should be >=, giving n = 2.

Moving n = 0 inside the loop resets the accumulator and gives 1 for any list; n = 1 stops counting; marks[1:] skips the first element and gives 1 for this list too, since 70 is the only one counted.

questions.q: What is the one thing that decides whether a test is black box or white box?
options: Whether it is run by hand or by an automated tool
Whether a tester or a developer runs it
Whether it is a functional or a non-functional test
Whether the internal structure of the item is known to the tester
questions.concept: Basis of black box versus white box
questions.why:
Black box testing is a method in which the internal structure, design and implementation of the item are not known to the tester; white box is one in which they are known. Nothing else is part of the definition.

Either kind can be manual or automated; a developer usually does white box testing but that is a consequence, not the definition; black box tests are usually functional but can be non-functional, so functional versus non-functional does not decide it.

questions.q: A quantity is valid from 1 to 99 inclusive, but the implementation reads `if qty >= 1 and qty < 99`. Boundary value analysis tests 0, 1, 2, 98, 99 and 100. Which of those six does the implementation get wrong?
questions.concept: Boundary value analysis exposing a fault
questions.why:
Boundary value analysis tests just below, at and just above each edge. The implementation calls 0 invalid, 1 valid, 2 valid, 98 valid, 99 invalid and 100 invalid. The specification makes 99 valid, so 99 is the single value where the two disagree, and the fix is `qty <= 99`.

0 and 100 lie outside the range and are correctly rejected; 1 is the lower edge and is correctly accepted; and rejecting 100 is right, not a fault.

questions.q:
total([5, 8, 2]) returns 10 where 15 is expected. A watch is set on the line `t = t + prices[i]`. What does it show, and where does the state first go wrong?

```python
def total(prices):
    t = 0
    for i in range(1, len(prices)):
        t = t + prices[i]
    return t
```
options: (i, t) = (1, 8) then (2, 10); wrong from the first pass, because index 0 is never added
(i, t) = (0, 5), (1, 13), (2, 15); nothing is wrong with the loop
(i, t) = (1, 8) then (2, 10); wrong only at the last pass, because the loop ends too early
(i, t) = (1, 5) then (2, 13); wrong from the first pass, because t starts at 5
questions.concept: Watching a variable to locate the defect
questions.why:
range(1, 3) gives i = 1 then 2, so the watch shows t = 0 + 8 = 8 and then t = 8 + 2 = 10. The state is already wrong on the first pass: t should be 5 there, from prices[0], and that element is never added at all. The defect is the off-by-one start, `range(1, ...)` where `range(len(prices))` was meant.

The second option is the corrected loop's trace; the third blames the end of the loop, which is right; the fourth blames the accumulator's starting value, which is 0 and correct.

questions.q: Four reports on a banking app: (a) balances are right but a page takes 30 seconds when 2,000 customers are logged in; (b) customers who are watched using the app cannot find the transfer button; (c) a logged-in customer opens another customer's statement by editing the address bar; (d) the function that adds two amounts returns 30 for 10 + 25. Which testing method finds each?
questions.concept: Classifying failures by testing method
questions.why:
Correct output but slow under load is performance testing; a fault found by observing real users at work is usability testing; one customer reading another's data is a confidentiality flaw, so security testing; and a single function returning the wrong value is unit testing, the only functional failure of the four.

System testing checks a whole build against its requirements rather than its behaviour under load; acceptance testing is the customer's final check, not an observed-user study; compatibility testing concerns different devices and browsers; and (d) is one function, not two parts being joined.

questions.q: Every function in a payment program has passed its unit tests, and the developer concludes that the program is free of defects. Which limitation of unit testing breaks that conclusion?
options: Unit tests check the user interface rather than the code.
Unit tests are written by developers, so they are never impartial.
Unit tests run before the code is compiled, so they see an older version.
Not all execution paths can be tested, and the amount and type of test data is limited.
questions.concept: Limits of unit testing
questions.why:
Unit testing feeds test data through a function's execution paths, and it is practically impossible to cover them all with the limited data available, so a passing suite shows only that the paths the data exercised behaved. It also says nothing about the parts working together: integration testing checks that, and system testing checks the whole build against the technical and functional requirements.

Unit tests do read the code, they run after compilation, and their authorship is not the limitation at issue.

checks.topic: Social vices: crime versus deviance, the theory lists, campus cultism and the kidnapping figures.

questions.q: A boy is repeatedly called a thief by his teachers and neighbours although he has stolen nothing; over time he begins to steal. Which theory of deviance best explains this?
questions.concept: Theories of deviance
questions.why: Labelling Theory holds that deviant behaviour is often a consequence of having a deviant-like label applied to a person, which is exactly what happens to the boy. Conflict Theory would explain his deviance by material inequality; Structural Functionalism says deviance plays a constructive role by helping society agree what is acceptable; Social Strain Typology classifies deviance by a person's adherence to cultural goals and belief in how to attain them.

questions.q: A man decides to rob a shop only after noting that it has no guard and judging that the likely gain outweighs the risk of arrest. Which theory of crime does this illustrate?
questions.concept: Theories of crime
questions.why: Rational Choice Theory argues that criminals weigh cost or risk against benefits when deciding whether to commit a crime, which is what the man does. Strain Theory would point to social structures pressuring him into crime; Social Learning Theory would require him to have observed and imitated others; Labelling Theory is a theory of deviance about labels applied to a person, not a weighing of risks.

questions.q: An action that violates social laws, as opposed to one that merely violates social norms and rules, is called:
questions.concept: Crime versus deviance
questions.why: Social vices are classified into two: committing a crime violates social laws, while deviant behaviour violates social norms and rules. Social vice is the wider category covering both. Deviance is the norm-breaking half, not the law-breaking half. Felony is the label given to a particular offence (allowing cult meetings in your residence), not the general term for law-breaking.

questions.q: Which of the following was NOT one of the original goals of the Pirates Confraternity founded at the University of Ibadan in the early 1950s?
options: To resist foreign norms nonviolently but intellectually
To resurrect the period of chivalry
To find a lasting solution to tribalism and ethnicity
To protect members from boys of rival groups
questions.concept: Origins of campus cultism
questions.why: The Pirates Confraternity, founded by Wole Soyinka and his friends as a social group with patriotic and philanthropic beliefs, had three major goals: to resist foreign norms nonviolently but intellectually, to resurrect the period of chivalry, and to find a lasting solution to tribalism and ethnicity. Protection from boys of rival cult groups is one of the reasons people join cults today, after such organisations grew to deadly proportions; it was not a founding goal.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the kidnapping figures in Nigeria is correct?
options: Reported kidnap cases rose from 838 in 2018 to 4,600 in 2022, roughly quadrupling
Reported kidnap cases fell from 11,858 in 2013 to 10,249 in 2014
Reported kidnap cases rose from 838 in 2018 to 1,676 in 2022, doubling
There were 4,600 kidnap cases in 2018, falling to 838 by 2022
questions.concept: Kidnapping figures
questions.why: In 2018 there were 838 reported kidnap cases; by 2022 the figure had risen to 4,600, an indication that cases had quadrupled. The 11,858 to 10,249 fall from 2013 to 2014 is the prison record for armed robbery, not kidnapping. The 1,676 figure would be a doubling, which understates the rise, and the last option reverses the direction of the change.

checks.topic: Future trends applied: Wasm, serverless behaviour, ML types, accessible markup and PWAs.

questions.q: ```html ``` A screen reader announces only "image". Which change makes the chart perceivable to that user?
questions.concept: Alternative text and the Perceivable principle
questions.why:
A screen reader cannot see the picture; it reads the alt attribute instead. Giving the image a meaningful alt text is the named example of the Perceivable principle: information presented so that every user can perceive it.

width changes only the layout; class is a styling hook that assistive technology ignores; wrapping the image in a div adds structure but still gives the reader nothing to say.

questions.q: A screen reader is pronouncing an English page with French pronunciation rules. Which attribute on the `<html>` element fixes this?
questions.concept: Declaring the page language for assistive technology
questions.why:
Assistive technology picks its pronunciation rules from the document's language, declared with lang on the root element: `<html lang="en">`. Without it the reader falls back to its own default language.

dir sets the text direction, left-to-right or right-to-left; charset belongs to a meta tag and names the character encoding, not the language; title is a tooltip and does not affect speech rules.

questions.q: One compiled WebAssembly build of a game runs unchanged in Chrome on a Windows laptop and in Safari on an iPhone. Which Wasm advantage is this?
questions.concept: The three advantages of WebAssembly
questions.why:
All major browsers support WebAssembly, so a single binary runs on desktop and mobile alike. That is the cross-platform compatibility advantage, whose named example is one web app working on both.

Speed is the near-native execution advantage; sandboxing is the security advantage that lets untrusted code run safely; statelessness is a serverless concept, not a Wasm one.

questions.q: A serverless function runs automatically each time a photo is uploaded to cloud storage and produces a thumbnail. Which serverless concept describes what starts the function?
questions.concept: Event-driven execution in serverless architecture
questions.why:
The upload is an event, and the function runs in response to it. Event-driven is the concept covering what triggers a function: HTTP requests, database changes and file uploads.

Stateless describes what the function must not keep between runs; a cold start is the delay when a function has been idle; vendor lock-in is a challenge about being tied to one provider.

questions.q: A serverless function runs 20,000 times in a month and each run takes 200 ms. Billing is ₦0.50 per second of compute used. What is the month's bill?
questions.concept: Pay-per-use cost of serverless compute
questions.why:
Total compute time is 20,000 × 0.2 s = 4,000 s. At ₦0.50 per second that is 4,000 × 0.5 = ₦2,000. Paying only for the seconds actually used is the cost-efficiency benefit.

₦10,000 charges a full second per run; ₦4,000 is the number of seconds, with the rate forgotten; ₦200 treats 200 ms as 0.02 s.

questions.q: A start-up built its whole backend on one cloud provider's proprietary function triggers and storage APIs, and now finds that moving to another provider means rewriting most of it. Which serverless challenge is this?
questions.concept: Vendor lock-in as a serverless challenge
questions.why:
Depending on one provider's proprietary services so that leaving means rewriting is vendor lock-in, one of the two named serverless challenges.

Cold starts are the other challenge, about latency after idleness; statelessness is a key concept, not a challenge; interoperability is listed among the challenges of ML and AI on the web, not of serverless.

questions.q: A model is trained on 10,000 emails, each already marked as spam or not spam, and then sorts new mail. Which type of machine learning is this?
questions.concept: Supervised versus unsupervised learning
questions.why:
The training data carries labels (spam, not spam) and the model learns to predict the label for new items. Learning from labelled data to classify is supervised learning, and the spam filter is its standard example.

Unsupervised learning uses unlabelled data to find groupings, such as clustering customers; computer vision interprets images and video; NLP is about understanding and generating language, and while emails are text, the defining feature here is the labels.

questions.q: A progressive web app rearranges its layout when the phone is turned from portrait to landscape. Which PWA feature is at work?
questions.concept: Responsive design in a PWA
questions.why:
Adapting the layout to the screen size and orientation is responsive design.

Service workers provide offline access, caching and push notifications; push notifications are messages delivered when the app is not open; progressive enhancement means the app works on basic browsers and gains features on capable ones.

questions.q: A blind student has each web page read aloud, or sent to a Braille display. Which assistive technology is this?
questions.concept: Assistive tools and who each serves
questions.why:
A screen reader converts the text and visual content of a page into speech or Braille output, which is exactly what a blind user needs.

Voice recognition takes speech as input from the user; a colour contrast tool checks that text stands out from its background for low-vision users; keyboard navigation serves users who cannot use a mouse.

questions.q: A smart doorbell classifies motion on the device itself instead of sending video to the cloud, so that it reacts with almost no delay. Which AI trend is this?
questions.concept: Edge AI among the future trends
questions.why:
Running the model close to where the data is generated, on the device rather than in the cloud, for low latency is Edge AI.

Explainable AI is about making a model's reasoning transparent; quantum machine learning is about using quantum computers for training; deep learning names the kind of model, not where it runs.

questions.q: Of artificial intelligence, machine learning and deep learning, which is the broadest category that contains the other two?
questions.concept: AI, ML and deep learning as nested categories
questions.why:
AI is the broad idea of machines doing tasks that need human intelligence. Machine learning is a subset of AI that learns from data, and deep learning is a subset of machine learning that uses many-layered neural networks. So AI contains both.

ML sits inside AI; deep learning is the narrowest of the three; NLP is a field within AI alongside computer vision, not the container of the others.

questions.q: What is a Progressive Web App (PWA)?
options: A web app that uses service workers and progressive enhancement to behave like an installed app, with offline access and push notifications
A mobile app compiled separately for Android and iOS from one code base
A website that upgrades itself to WebAssembly on capable browsers
A serverless function that renders web pages on demand
questions.concept: Definition of a Progressive Web App
questions.why:
A PWA is a web application that combines the reach of the web with the feel of a mobile app: service workers give offline access, caching and push notifications, and progressive enhancement means it works for every browser and improves on advanced devices. Twitter Lite and Flipkart are named examples.

Separately compiled native apps are what a PWA avoids, which is where the cost saving comes from; WebAssembly is unrelated to PWAs; serverless functions run on the provider's servers, not in the user's browser.

checks.topic: Active listening's three benefits and six techniques, the note-taking tips, and deductive versus inductive reasoning.

questions.q: In a meeting, Yemi keeps cutting in with her reply before the speaker has finished his point, and he is left feeling unheard. Which technique for becoming a more active listener has she failed to apply?
questions.concept: Techniques for active listening applied to a scenario
questions.why:
Avoid Interrupting means letting the speaker finish their thoughts before responding, because interruptions hinder the flow of communication and make the speaker feel unheard.

Minimise Distractions concerns the environment, not cutting in; Maintain Eye Contact is a non-verbal cue of attention; Paraphrase and Summarise is restating the message to check understanding.

questions.q: Ada tries to write down every word of a lecture, falls behind, and ends up with pages of notes she cannot use for revision. Which note-taking tip has she ignored?
options: Use headings and subheadings to structure notes
Do not write verbatim; capture main ideas, key concepts and supporting evidence
Divide the page into cues, notes and a summary
questions.concept: Note-taking tips applied to a fault
questions.why:
The tip is to listen attentively and not write what you hear verbatim, but to jot down main ideas, key concepts and supporting evidence in clear, simple sentences, which prevents information overload.

Headings and subheadings help you find information later; writing materials are a separate preparation tip; dividing the page is the Cornell method, which does not by itself stop transcription.

questions.q: Two roommates are in a dispute. A friend listens to each in turn until both acknowledge the other's perspective and they find common ground. Which named benefit of active listening is this?
questions.concept: The three benefits of active listening
questions.why:
Conflict Resolution is the benefit under which active listening lets individuals acknowledge each other's perspectives, a crucial step in finding common ground and resolving disputes.

Enhanced Understanding is grasping the words plus the emotions, intentions and context; Problem Solving is giving informed solutions after comprehending a problem's details; improved retention is a payoff of note-taking, not one of the three headings.

questions.q: Bola hands in a formal essay containing 'w/' for 'with' and an arrow for 'leads to'. Which caution about abbreviations and symbols has she ignored?
options: They must follow a standard list shared by all students
They should replace full sentences wherever possible
They belong in personal notes and may not be tolerated in formal writing
They may only be used in the cue column of Cornell notes
questions.concept: Abbreviations in notes versus formal writing
questions.why:
A system of abbreviations and symbols is for personal notes that are not turned in or submitted; abbreviations and symbols may not be tolerated in formal writings.

The system is personal, not standardised; it is meant to speed up note-taking without sacrificing clarity, not to replace sentences in formal work; nothing restricts symbols to the cue column.

questions.q: Which form of reasoning starts with specific observations in order to make broader generalisations?
questions.concept: Inductive versus deductive reasoning in presentations
questions.why:
Inductive reasoning starts with specific observations to make broader generalisations; deductive reasoning draws specific conclusions from general premises.

Strawman arguments and hasty generalisations are named logical fallacies to be avoided in a presentation, not forms of reasoning to be applied.

checks.topic: The Young modulus beam experiment: definitions, the depression formula, apparatus and the gradient.

questions.q:
A copper beam loaded at its centre gives these dial-gauge readings:

m (g):   50    100   200   300   400   500
Y (mm):  0.04  0.08  0.16  0.25  0.33  0.41

Using the points at 100 g and 500 g, what is the gradient of the Y (m) against m (kg) graph in SI units?
questions.concept: Gradient of depression against load in SI units
questions.why:
Convert both axes: 0.41 mm = 0.41 × 10⁻³ m, 0.08 mm = 0.08 × 10⁻³ m, 500 g = 0.500 kg, 100 g = 0.100 kg. Gradient s = ΔY/Δm = (0.41 − 0.08) × 10⁻³/(0.500 − 0.100) = 0.33 × 10⁻³/0.400 = 8.25 × 10⁻⁴ m/kg.

8.25 × 10⁻⁷ converts Y to metres but leaves m in grams; 0.825 converts m to kilograms but leaves Y in millimetres; 1.21 × 10³ is the reciprocal Δm/ΔY.

questions.q: A beam of length ℓ = 80.0 cm, thickness d = 0.80 cm and breadth b = 25.0 mm rests on two mounts. Its Y against m graph has gradient s = 8.25 × 10⁻⁴ m/kg. Take g = 9.8 m/s². What is the Young modulus of the material?
questions.concept: Young modulus from the gradient and the beam dimensions
questions.why:
In metres: ℓ = 0.800 m, d = 0.0080 m, b = 0.0250 m. From Y = mgℓ³/(4Ebd³) the gradient is s = gℓ³/(4Ebd³), so E = gℓ³/(4bd³s) = (9.8 × 0.512)/(4 × 0.0250 × 5.12 × 10⁻⁷ × 8.25 × 10⁻⁴) = 5.018/(4.224 × 10⁻¹¹) = 1.19 × 10¹¹ Pa = 119 GPa, close to copper's accepted 120 GPa.

475 GPa drops the factor 4; 9.9 GPa keeps the 48 from Y = mgℓ³/(48EI) after already substituting I = bd³/12, so the 12 is counted twice; 12.2 GPa cubes b instead of d.

questions.q: A wire 2.0 m long with cross-sectional area 2.0 mm² extends by 0.50 mm under a tension of 40 N. What is the Young modulus of the wire?
questions.concept: Young modulus from stress over strain
questions.why:
Stress = F/A = 40/(2.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 2.0 × 10⁷ Pa. Strain = Δℓ/ℓ = 0.50 × 10⁻³/2.0 = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴, no unit. E = stress/strain = 2.0 × 10⁷/2.5 × 10⁻⁴ = 8.0 × 10¹⁰ Pa.

2.0 × 10⁷ Pa is the stress alone; 4.0 × 10¹⁰ Pa divides the stress by the extension in metres instead of by the strain; 8.0 × 10⁴ Pa leaves the area as 2.0 instead of converting mm² to m².

questions.q: A beam of thickness 0.50 cm shows a central depression of 0.48 mm under a 500 g load. It is replaced by a beam of the same material, length and breadth but thickness 1.00 cm. What depression does the same load produce?
questions.concept: Effect of thickness on the depression
questions.why:
Y = mgℓ³/(4Ebd³), so with everything else fixed Y ∝ 1/d³. Doubling d divides the depression by 2³ = 8: Y = 0.48/8 = 0.06 mm. This is why d is the measurement that matters most.

0.24 mm halves Y as if it fell linearly with d; 0.12 mm divides by 4, treating d as squared; 0.96 mm doubles Y, as though a thicker beam sagged more.

questions.q: Before any mass is added the dial gauge already reads 0.03 mm, and the student does not zero it. What does this do to the graph of Y against m?
options: Gradient increased, line still through the origin
Line curves upward at large loads
questions.concept: Effect of a dial-gauge zero error on the graph
questions.why:
A zero error adds the same 0.03 mm to every reading, so each point is lifted by the same amount: the line keeps its slope but no longer passes through the origin, cutting the Y-axis at 0.03 mm. Because E is taken from the gradient, the result is unaffected provided the gradient is measured from the best-fit line and not from a single (m, Y) pair.

A constant offset cannot change the gradient in either direction; curvature at large loads is the sign of exceeding the proportional limit, not of a zero error.

recapCandidates.topic: An integral of a rate is a SIGNED accumulation, so it returns displacement and never distance; the repair is to split at the zeros of v and add magnitudes, never to take a modulus at the end. And the constant of integration is a physical quantity the rate cannot contain — v(0) in kinematics, the fixed cost C(0) in economics — which is also why the extra cost between two outputs needs no fixed cost at all.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Every early example has a positive integrand, so the signed nature of the integral stays invisible until v changes sign; and the attempted repair, taking the modulus after integrating, cannot recover a cancellation that has already happened inside the integral.
whyQuestions: Why does ∫₃⁷ r(t)dt come out in litres when r is in litres per minute — and what in that unit calculation tells you the answer is an amount rather than a rate?
Why is ∫₀⁴ v dt the displacement rather than the distance, when the same integral over a positive velocity gives both?
Why does |∫₀⁴ v dt| fail to fix it, and what exactly has been lost by the time you reach the modulus?
Why can a(t), known perfectly for every instant, still not tell you v(t) — and what is the physical name of the missing information in the kinematics case and in the marginal-cost case?
Why must the fixed cost be added to get C(5), yet left out entirely to get the extra cost of going from q = 2 to q = 5 — and why is it the same fact about constants that answers both halves?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
States the net change theorem with 'net' doing real work: ∫ₐᵇ r dt = f(b) − f(a) is a balance in which intervals where r < 0 subtract from those where r > 0, which is exactly what displacement means and exactly what distance must not do; confirms the reading dimensionally, (units of r)x(units of t).
Gives the procedure for distance rather than just the formula ∫|v|dt — locate the zeros of v, integrate each sub-interval separately, take the modulus of each result, add — and says why the modulus must go inside: after integrating, the forward and backward motion have already cancelled.
Treats the constant of integration as a physical fact, not notation: antidifferentiation fixes the function only up to +C, so v(0) or C(0) supplies information the rate does not contain; then closes the loop by noting the constant vanishes from every difference, so it matters for a level and is irrelevant to a change.
recapCandidates.workedExample: v(t) = t² − 4t + 3 m/s on [0,4], s(0) = 0. Since v = (t − 1)(t − 3), v > 0 on [0,1), v < 0 on (1,3), v > 0 on (3,4]. Displacement = ∫₀⁴ v dt = [t³/3 − 2t² + 3t]₀⁴ = 4/3 m — nothing further is needed, the integral has already accounted for the backward leg. Total distance: split at t = 1 and t = 3 to get +4/3, −4/3 and +4/3, so the distance is 4 m. The wrong approach, |∫₀⁴ v dt| = 4/3, is the displacement wearing a modulus sign; the split shows the middle leg's −4/3 silently annihilating the first leg's +4/3, and the cheap check is that distance must exceed |displacement| whenever v changes sign. Splitting anywhere else fails: at t = 2 the two pieces are +2/3 and +2/3, giving 4/3 again, because the zeros of v are the only points where cancellation can begin. The same fact in money: with MC(q) = 3q² − 4q + 10 and fixed cost ₦50, C(q) = q³ − 2q² + 10q + 50, so C(5) = ₦175 (a level, fixed cost included) while the extra cost from q = 2 to q = 5 is ∫₂⁵ MC dq = 125 − 20 = ₦105 (a change, fixed cost cancelled). ₦155 pays the rent twice; MC(5) − MC(2) = ₦51 differences the rate instead of accumulating it, the exact analogue of reading v(4) when asked how far the particle went.

recapCandidates.topic: A transformer is not an amplifier. It buys voltage with current at an exactly equal rate, V₁I₁ = V₂I₂, so the turns ratio multiplies voltage by N₂/N₁ and divides current by the same factor — but it transforms a load resistance by the SQUARE of that ratio, (N₁/N₂)²R. And none of it functions on DC, because every volt it produces comes from dΦ/dt.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: The first questions asked about transformers are voltage questions, which the turns ratio answers without ever mentioning current, so the amplifier intuition survives; the power balance then arrives as a second formula to memorise rather than as the reason the first cannot mean what the student thought.
whyQuestions: Why does the transformer equation V₂/V₁ = N₂/N₁ hold at all — what is the same for both coils, and what does each turn contribute?
Why must the secondary current go down when the secondary voltage goes up, and what statement of physics fixes the two ratios as exact reciprocals rather than merely opposite in tendency?

Why is a load resistance transformed by the square of the turns ratio when voltage and current are each transformed by only the first power — and can you get the square out of the two rules rather than recalling it?

Why does connecting an 8 Ω loudspeaker directly to an amplifier of 800 Ω internal resistance deliver less power to it than putting a lossy transformer in between, even though the transformer can only waste energy?
Why does a transformer produce nothing at all on DC — and, given that answer, why does the output frequency equal the input frequency no matter what the turns ratio is?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
Derives the turns ratio rather than asserting it: one alternating flux threads every turn of both windings, so each turn carries the same emf −dΦ/dt, giving V₁ = −N₁dΦ/dt and V₂ = −N₂dΦ/dt and hence V₁/N₁ = V₂/N₂; then names the current ratio as a separate statement coming from conservation of energy.
Obtains the resistance rule from the other two in front of the listener: V₁/I₁ = (N₁/N₂)²(V₂/I₂), one factor from the voltage and one from the current, and connects it to impedance matching for maximum power transfer.
Identifies the transformer as a Faraday's-law device throughout, so the AC requirement is a consequence, not an extra rule: steady DC gives dΦ/dt = 0 and zero output; the turns ratio scales the size of the emf but not the rate at which the flux reverses, so the frequency is untouched and a transformer cannot rectify.
recapCandidates.workedExample: A 60 W, 24 V soldering iron run from 240 V rms mains through an ideal transformer with a 1200-turn primary. Turns: N₂ = 1200 x 24/240 = 120 (fewer volts out means fewer turns out; 12 000 inverts the ratio). Currents: in the iron I₂ = 60/24 = 2.5 A, but the mains current comes from the power balance, not the turns ratio — P₁ = P₂ = 60 W so I₁ = 60/240 = 0.25 A. The voltage fell by 10 and the current rose by 10, and 240 x 0.25 = 24 x 2.5 = 60 W on both sides, which is itself the answer to 'does it amplify?'. Resistance: the iron is V₂²/P = 9.6 Ω, but the mains sees V₁/I₁ = 240/0.25 = 960 Ω = 10² x 9.6 — the square appears because the source supplies 10x the voltage AND 1/10 the current, and 10 divided by 1/10 is 100; 96 Ω uses the first power. Same physics at scale: 100 kW down a 4.0 Ω line at 1.0 kV means I = 100 A and I²R = 40 kW wasted; at 10 kV, I = 10 A and the waste is 400 W — a hundredfold saving for a tenfold voltage, because V enters twice, once in I = P/V and again because the heating is quadratic. The delivered 100 kW is identical in both cases: the transformer bought nothing, it just moved the power as a small current at high voltage.
